evidence.passage:
For Noether's second theorem, we consider those variational symmetries (called ''[[Gauge symmetry (mathematics)|gauge symmetries]]'') which are parametrized linearly by a set of arbitrary functions and their derivatives. These variations have the generic form <math display="block">\delta_\lambda u^\sigma = R^\sigma_a \lambda^a + R^{\sigma,i}_{a}\lambda^a_{i} + \dots + R^{\sigma,i_1...i_s}_a \lambda^a_{i_1...i_s}
= \sum_{|I|=0}^s R^{\sigma,I}_a \lambda^a_I,</math>where the coefficients <math>R^{\sigma,I}_a</math> can depend on the independent and dependent variables as well as the derivatives of the latter up to some finite order, the <math>\lambda^a =  \lambda^a (x)</math> are arbitrarily specifiable functions of the independent variables, and the Latin indices <math>a,b,\dots</math> take the values <math>1,\dots,q</math>, where <math>q</math> is some positive integer.

For these variations to be (exact, i.e. not quasi-) gauge symmetries of the Lagrangian, it is necessary that <math>\delta_\lambda L = 0</math> for all possible choices of the functions <math>\lambda^a (x)</math>. If the variations are quasi-symmetries, it is then necessary that the current also depends linearly and differentially on the arbitrary functions, i.e. then <math>\delta_\lambda L =d_i K^i_\lambda</math>, where<math display="block">K^i_\lambda = K^i_a \lambda^a + K^{i,j}_a \lambda^a_{j} + K^{i,j_1j_2}_a \lambda^a_{j_1j_2}\dots</math>For simplicity, we will assume that all gauge symmetries are exact symmetries, but the general case is handled similarly.

=== Noether's second theorem ===
The statement of Noether's second theorem is that whenever given a Lagrangian <math display="inline">L</math> as above that admits gauge symmetries <math>\delta_\lambda u^\sigma </math> parametrized linearly by <math>q</math> arbitrary functions and their derivatives, then there exist <math>q</math> linear differential relations between the Euler-Lagrange equations of <math display="inline">L</math>.

Let ''X'' be a [[finite set]] and let ''G'' be a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] of [[permutation]]s of ''X'' (or a [[Finite group|finite]] [[symmetry group]] that [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] on ''X''). The set ''X'' may represent a finite set of beads, and ''G'' may be a chosen group of permutations of the beads. For example, if ''X'' is a [[necklace (combinatorics)|necklace]] of ''n'' beads in a circle, then [[rotational symmetry]] is relevant so ''G'' is the [[cyclic group]] ''C<sub>n</sub>'', while if ''X'' is a [[bracelet (combinatorics)|bracelet]] of ''n'' beads in a circle, rotations and [[Reflection symmetry|reflections]] are relevant so ''G'' is the [[dihedral group]] ''D<sub>n</sub>'' of order 2''n''. Suppose further that ''Y'' is a finite set of colors — the colors of the beads — so that ''Y<sup>X</sup>'' is the set of colored arrangements of beads (more formally: ''Y<sup>X</sup>'' is the set of functions <math>X \to Y</math>.) Then the group ''G'' acts on ''Y<sup>X</sup>''. The Pólya enumeration theorem counts the number of orbits under ''G'' of colored arrangements of beads by the following formula:

:<math>\left |Y^X/G \right | = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} m^{c(g)}</math>

where <math>m=|Y|</math> is the number of colors and ''c''(''g'') is the number of [[Cyclic permutation|cycles]] of the group element ''g'' when considered as a permutation of ''X''.

The statement of Jacobson–Morozov relies on the following preliminary notions: an sl<sub>2</sub>-triple in a [[semi-simple Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak g</math> (throughout in this article, over a field of [[characteristic zero]]) is a [[homomorphism]] of Lie algebras <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \to \mathfrak g</math>. Equivalently, it is a triple <math>e, f, h</math> of elements in <math>\mathfrak g</math> satisfying the relations 
:<math>[h,e] = 2e, \quad [h,f] = -2f, \quad [e,f] = h. </math>
An element <math>x \in \mathfrak g</math> is called nilpotent, if the [[endomorphism]] <math>[x, -] : \mathfrak g \to \mathfrak g</math> (known as the [[adjoint representation]]) is a [[nilpotent endomorphism]]. It is an elementary fact that for any sl<sub>2</sub>-triple <math>(e, f, h)</math>, ''e'' must be nilpotent. The Jacobson–Morozov theorem states that, conversely, any nilpotent non-zero element <math>e \in \mathfrak g</math> can be extended to an sl<sub>2</sub>-triple.<ref>{{harvtxt|Bourbaki|2007|loc=Ch. VIII, §11, Prop. 2}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Jacobson|1979|loc=Ch. III, §11, Theorem 17}}</ref>

In [[mathematics]], '''Hartogs's theorem''' is a fundamental result of [[Friedrich Hartogs]] in the theory of [[Function of several complex variables|several complex variables]]. Roughly speaking, it states that a 'separately analytic' function is continuous. More precisely, if <math>F:{\textbf{C}}^n \to {\textbf{C}}</math> is a  function which is [[analytic function|analytic]] in each variable ''z''<sub>''i''</sub>, 1 ≤ ''i'' ≤ ''n'', while the other variables are held constant,  then ''F'' is a [[continuous function]].

A [[corollary]]  is that the function ''F'' is then in fact an analytic function in the ''n''-variable sense (i.e. that locally it has a [[Taylor expansion]]). Therefore, 'separate analyticity' and 'analyticity' are coincident notions, in the theory of several complex variables.
